analysis.one_liner: Lets the IRS write rules requiring disclosure of political spending by certain tax-exempt nonprofits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2017, annual spending bills have included a rider that bars the IRS from writing any rules about political activity by certain tax-exempt 'social welfare' nonprofits. Those rules are the legal path to requiring these groups to disclose who funds their political ads and campaigns. H.R. 327 would have wiped out that restriction for fiscal year 2021, freeing the IRS to act. The bill went nowhere: it was referred to the tax-writing committee and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would learn which organizations and donors are behind political ads and campaign spending that currently can be run anonymously through tax-exempt groups. Campaign-finance watchdog groups and small donors in transparent groups also gain a clearer field.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes a provision in the FY2021 appropriations law that blocks the IRS from issuing any regulation or guidance on the standard for whether civic nonprofits are operated exclusively for social welfare — the legal precondition for tightening disclosure of their political activity.

By restoring the IRS's ability to act, the bill opens a path to 'bring transparency to the political activity of certain nonprofit organizations,' as its title states — meaning voters could see who is paying for political messages delivered under a nonprofit label.

analysis.who_pays: Tax-exempt organizations that engage in political spending without disclosing donors, and the donors behind them, who would face new IRS rules requiring disclosure. No ordinary taxpayer pays anything.
analysis.who_pays_short: Anonymous political spenders and their donors

drawbacks.text: The bill is narrow and indirect: it only nullifies the restriction for fiscal year 2021, and even then it merely permits the IRS to write rules — it does not itself require disclosure. Any IRS guidance would face years of rulemaking, legal challenges, and possible repeal by a future Congress.

Critics of donor-disclosure requirements for nonprofits argue that public disclosure can expose small-dollar supporters of controversial causes to harassment, a tradeoff an honest supporter would acknowledge even while favoring disclosure of large political spenders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — voters knowing who funds political messaging disguised as nonprofit activity — is real and directly relevant to self-government, while the costs fall on a narrow set of political spenders. The bill's main weakness is design, not substance: a one-fiscal-year repeal is a small, temporary lever, and it depends entirely on the IRS subsequently writing rules it had been blocked from writing. An honest supporter would concede the bill alone changes little unless followed by actual IRS action.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jason Crow introduced the bill on January 15, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which handles tax and IRS matters.
Four House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — and the House never voted on the bill for the rest of the 117th Congress.

The bill's stated purpose was to repeal the appropriations rider that had barred the IRS from issuing rules about the political activity of tax-exempt social welfare nonprofits, the mechanism commonly described as 'dark money' spending.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The organizations and donors who spend on politics through tax-exempt nonprofits without disclosing their funding are better off, because the IRS remains barred from writing disclosure rules by the appropriations riders this bill would have lifted. Voters did not gain the transparency the bill offered.

for.name: Rep. Jason Crow
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let the IRS write political-spending disclosure rules for tax-exempt nonprofits.

for.name: Reps. John Sarbanes, Ted Lieu, Jim McGovern, and Katie Porter
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all four were Democrats.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under the House rules
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for two years.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration; the bill never left committee.

against.name: Anonymous political spenders and their donors
against.role: Funders of issue ads through tax-exempt nonprofits
against.what_they_did: Beneficiaries of the appropriations riders the bill targeted; outside advocacy by these interests is a common factor in keeping IRS disclosure rules off the table, though the record contains no direct action on this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill (1 sponsor plus 4 Democratic cosponsors), and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the opposition is a matter of inference rather than record.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt 'dark money' groups (501(c)(4) social welfare organizations active in politics)
industries.note: The bill would free the IRS to write rules that could force these groups to disclose the donors behind their political spending. Their advantage today is spending on elections without public attribution, which comes at the direct cost of voters' ability to see who is paying.

industries.industry: Political consulting and media firms funded through anonymous nonprofit grants
industries.note: Their business depends on anonymous money flowing through tax-exempt groups; donor disclosure rules made possible by the bill would raise scrutiny of that channel. Ordinary voters would gain visibility into who funds the ads they see.
